summary: This informational RFC provides a threat analysis of the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP), examining how it might be attacked.

eli5.summary: A safety inspection of a new system, listing the ways someone might try to break or abuse it.

questions: what are the security threats to lisp
how can lisp map-reply be abused
subtitle: A catalogue of how attackers could abuse the Locator/ID Separation Protocol if it were deployed on the open Internet.

tldr.problem: LISP was specified without a full assessment of how it could be attacked when deployed in a public, non-trustable environment such as the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a threat model (modes of attackers and eleven threat categories), then walks through the LISP features and messages an attacker can exploit, and finally discusses mitigations.
tldr.outcome: Most threats can be mitigated by careful deployment, filtering, rate limiting, authentication of mapping messages and by verifying opportunistically learned information before relying on it.

today: RFC 7835 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. It analyzes the LISP specifications of its time, chiefly RFC 6830, and notes that additional threats may be discovered while deployment continues.

sections.title: Scope of the Threat Analysis
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) is specified in RFC 6830. This RFC assesses the security threats to the LISP specifications if LISP is deployed in the Internet, a public non-trustable environment. It has three parts: a general threat model, the LISP techniques attackers can use to build attacks, and mitigation techniques.

It focuses on LISP unicast, including Interworking (RFC 6832), the Map-Server (RFC 6833) and Map-Versioning (RFC 6834). It does not cover every possible use of LISP or threats due to specific implementations, and it does not discuss differences between IPv4 and IPv6. Further threats may be discovered while deployment continues, and the reader is assumed to know the base LISP documents.
sections.eli5: Before a new playground opens, someone walks around looking for places a kid could get hurt or a bully could cause trouble. This is that walk-through for LISP.

sections.title: The Threat Model
sections.content:
Attackers can be anywhere on the Internet, inside or outside LISP sites, and may work alone or collude. The RFC classifies them by how they operate, and the modes can be combined: on-path versus off-path, internal versus external, live versus time-shifted, and control-plane versus data-plane. A time-shifted attacker's attack stays active after it disconnects. A control-plane attacker uses functions such as the mapping system.

Attacks fall into eleven categories that can also be combined: replay, packet manipulation, packet interception and suppression, spoofing, rogue, denial of service (DoS), performance, intrusion, amplification, passive monitoring and multi-category attacks. Because LISP encapsulates packets, spoofing comes in two forms: inner address spoofing forges the source EID, and outer address spoofing forges the source RLOC. Using both makes the attacker hard to identify.

In an amplification attack the target's response traffic is larger than what the attacker sends. The RFC notes that the data plane can be several orders of magnitude faster than the control plane at processing packets, which can be used to overload the control plane through the data plane.
sections.eli5: The inspectors sort troublemakers by where they stand and how long they stay, and sort the trouble by type, such as sending fake letters, copying old ones or flooding the mailroom.

sections.title: Attack Vectors in the Data Plane
sections.content:
Gleaning lets an xTR learn an EID-to-RLOC mapping straight from encapsulated data packets and Map-Requests. An off-path attacker who injects a packet with a spoofed inner address may divert traffic meant for that EID while the gleaned entry is used. A spoofed outer address can redirect traffic to a victim and cause a DoS or performance attack. Sending a packet for each address of an uncached prefix can trigger a Map-Request per packet even if gleaning is off. RFC 6830 recommends keeping gleaned entries for only a few seconds, which limits the attack.

Locator Status Bits (the L bit in the LISP header) report the status of the RLOCs. A forged value can declare all RLOCs unreachable, concentrate traffic on one RLOC, or send packets to unreachable ones. The Map-Version bit can make an xTR send Map-Requests or Solicit-Map-Requests, enabling DoS, amplification or spoofing. The Nonce-Present and Echo-Nonce bits used for RLOC reachability can be abused to make an xTR believe another is reachable, or to make the ETR keep changing the nonce it echoes.

The 24-bit Instance ID can be used by control-plane or data-plane attackers for intrusion attacks. Proxy-ITRs and Proxy-ETRs used for interworking are subject to attacks similar to ITRs and ETRs, and like any proxy can be used to hide where an attack comes from.
sections.eli5: Some shortcuts in LISP let a router believe what a packet says about itself. A liar could trick the router into sending mail to the wrong address or flooding one mailbox.

sections.title: Attack Vectors in the Mapping System
sections.content:
Map-Request messages sent at a high rate can overload the mapping system, grow the state held by a Map-Resolver or use up ETR CPU, and if the Map-Reply is larger than the request, amplify the attack. Map-Records appended to a Map-Request are installed in the target's cache, so forged or many de-aggregated mappings can pollute it.

Map-Reply risk depends on the 64-bit nonce echoed from the Map-Request. With a good random source and rejection of invalid nonces, off-path attack is limited, but the nonce does not validate the reply's contents. An attacker that gets a valid reply accepted can inject forged mappings. A valid but malicious ETR can also overclaim a prefix, for example answering for 192.0.2.0/24 when it owns only 192.0.2.0/25.

Map-Register messages are protected by an authentication mechanism, so only a compromised ETR can register, but such an ETR can overclaim or de-aggregate its prefix. A compromised Map Server can accept invalid registrations. Map-Notify messages are protected by a nonce, which makes injecting a false acknowledgement difficult.
sections.eli5: The address book that tells routers where everyone lives can be flooded with questions, or fed fake entries. A lying neighbor can also claim to own more houses than they really do.

sections.title: Privacy and Mitigation
sections.content:
The RFC does not try to identify privacy issues in LISP, since privacy definitions vary, but notes that the threats could play a role in privacy threats. LISP mappings are public in an Internet deployment and reveal information about the infrastructure and reachability of LISP sites, such as the addresses of edge routers.

Most threats can be mitigated by careful deployment and configuration, such as filters, by enabling only the features a deployment needs, and by verifying information from third parties. The control plane is the most critical part. LISP already has authentication for mapping registration, which combined with LISP-SEC strongly mitigates threats in non-trustable environments, and an authentication data field for Map-Request and Encapsulated Control messages whose exact technique is still to be defined. Authentication must be used, whenever possible, for Map-Request and Map-Reply messages and for exchanges inside the mapping system.

Filters and rate limiting as proposed in RFC 6830 mitigate most threats, and control-plane actions triggered by data-plane events should be rate limited. Opportunistically learned information, such as from LSBs or gleaning, should be used with care until verified: an LSB reachability change should trigger a rate-limited reachability test, and a gleaned entry should be used only for the flow that triggered it until verified.
sections.eli5: The fixes are like locks and sensible rules: only turn on what you need, check who is really asking, slow down anyone who asks too fast, and do not trust a stranger's note until you have checked it.
